newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia launches offset programme for new aircraft.
newsitem.headline: Croatia launches offset programme for new aircraft.

text.p: Croatia Airlines signed an agreement with gas turbine works Tvornica Plinskih Turbina (TPT) on Friday, launching an offset programme designed to boost Croatian manufacturers' exports to Europe.

Earlier this year the airline ordered six medium-range A319s from Airbus Industrie with engines from French-American aircraft engine maker CFM International, and agreed that some 40 percent of the total cost, put at over $300 million, would be offset by exports of Croatian goods.
TPT will supply $15 million worth of engine components -- compression chamber parts, disks and blades -- to CFM, company officials told a news conference.
For this it would get technical assistance from foreign partners, CFM and Airbus, for upgrading computerised production lines and additional training.
"One of the main purposes of this agreement is to introduce new technologies or develop existing ones," said Matija Katicic, board president of the national flag carrier.
This was aimed at helping local firms set up smaller plants to manufacture components for the aircraft industry, he said.
Other companies including shipyards such as Pula's Uljanik were also expected to join the airline's offset programme with their goods, officials said.

"Linking imports of capital goods to exports of Croatian products is aimed at narrowing the existing trade deficit. It may be a novelty here, but even the most developed countries use it," said Assistant Economy Minister Milan Cuvalo.

This would not affect financing of the purchase by Croatia from its revenues, Katicic said, but added that a commission of between one and 4-4.5 percent on individual export deals would be handy when it came to annuity payments.
A deal on a loan from a consortium of European banks was close to being wrapped up, an airline source told Reuters.

Croatia Airlines had a net loss of $3.4 million in 1995 on revenue of $95.4 million, after high loan costs swallowed most of its revenue rise of over $10 million. It hoped to break even last year but no results are yet available.

Private investors control around eight percent of Croatia Airlines. The government has made a first step towards its further privatisation by including a 27-percent stake of the company in its $2.3 billion mass voucher scheme.
The airline hopes that these shares may eventually find a buyer among leading European carriers such as Lufthansa or Swissair to improve its competitive position.
